summary: Monaco is a city-state on the French Riviera, ruled by the House of Grimaldi, and is known for the Monte Carlo casino, the Formula One Grand Prix and its concentration of wealthy residents.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Monaco has been a Catholic country since the Middle Ages; the House of Grimaldi, which has ruled since 1297, has always been Catholic, and the constitution makes Catholicism the state religion. The feast of the patron saint, Saint Devota, and the High Mass on National Day (19 November) are important state ceremonies, and the 1956 wedding of Rainier III and Grace Kelly was also held in Monaco Cathedral.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Foreigners make up a high proportion of Monaco's residents, many from more secularized European countries such as France and the United Kingdom, bringing a secular way of life and gradually raising the proportion of people with no religion.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: These include the Anglican Church (mainly serving British residents), Greek and Russian Orthodox churches, and other Protestant groups. As a wealthy international place of residence, Monaco has attracted residents from all over the world, and so has a diverse range of Christian denominations.

ranking.name: Judaism
ranking.description: The Jewish community consists mainly of Jews who moved in from North Africa and Europe after World War II, and Monaco has a synagogue. During World War II, under pressure from Vichy France and Germany, Monaco arrested some Jewish refugees, and in 2015 Prince Albert II formally apologized for this.

religion.background: Monaco accepted Christianity after Roman times. According to legend, the body of Saint Devota (Sainte Dévote), a woman martyred in the 4th century, drifted to Monaco by boat, and she became Monaco's patron saint, with a festival held every year on 27 January. In 1297 the House of Grimaldi seized Monaco and has ruled it ever since. Monaco has been a Catholic country since the Middle Ages, the Diocese of Monaco was established in 1887, and the constitution makes Catholicism the state religion. In recent years, when parliament discussed relaxing rules on issues such as abortion, Prince Albert II expressed reservations on the grounds of Catholicism's status as state religion, showing that Catholicism still influences national policy today.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: Monaco is surrounded by France, and after the 19th century its economic and administrative ties with France became ever closer, especially after it ceded Menton and Roquebrune in 1861. French is the sole official language, used in government, schools, courts and the media, and the great majority of residents also use French as their main language.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: Monaco is adjacent to Italy's Liguria region, was historically influenced by the Republic of Genoa, and was a protectorate of the Kingdom of Sardinia from 1815 to 1860. Large numbers of Italians live and work there, making Italian very common in daily life; the traditional Monegasque language also derives from a Genoese dialect.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: Monaco is a place of residence for international millionaires and celebrities, and many British and American residents and business people live there; international events such as the Monte Carlo casino and Formula One racing also make English an important language of business and tourism.

language.history: The original inhabitants of Monaco spoke Monégasque, a branch of the Genoese dialect belonging to the Ligurian language. After Monaco ceded Menton and Roquebrune to France in 1861, its relations with France became closer, and French gradually became the language of administration and daily life. The 1962 constitution made French the official language. In the 20th century Monégasque nearly disappeared; from the 1970s the government made it a compulsory school subject, and Monégasque has since experienced a certain revival, and today street signs often show both French and Monégasque.

ranking.name: Barbagiuan
ranking.description: Fried dumplings of pastry filled with Swiss chard leaves, spinach, cheese and rice, the national dish of Monaco. The crust is crisp, and the filling has the aroma of vegetables and cheese.
ranking.history: Barbagiuan means "Uncle John" in Monégasque, and folk legend says it was invented by an uncle named John, though this cannot be verified. It resembles the fried dumplings of Liguria and the Nice area, reflecting Monaco's roots in Genoese culture. It is a traditional treat for Monaco's National Day (19 November), and Monegasques also make it at festivals such as the Feast of Saint Devota.

ranking.name: Socca (chickpea pancake)
ranking.description: A thin pancake made from a batter of chickpea flour, water and olive oil, baked in a wood-fired oven on a large copper plate, sprinkled with black pepper and eaten hot. It is crisp and charred outside and soft inside, with the nutty flavor of chickpeas.
ranking.history: Socca originated on the coast around Nice and Liguria, where Genoa calls it farinata. Legend traces it to the time of the medieval naval battles between Genoa and Pisa, but there is no firm evidence. Chickpea flour is cheap and keeps well, and it was an inexpensive food for coastal port workers and fishermen. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, vendors in the markets of Nice and Monaco pushed ovens around selling socca, and today it is still a representative street snack of the Riviera.

ranking.name: Stocafi
ranking.description: A dish of soaked Norwegian dried cod stewed with tomatoes, olives, onion, garlic and white wine. It has a rich, salty and savory flavor and is a traditional home-style dish of Monaco.
ranking.history: The name Stocafi comes from the dried cod of northern Europe (stockfish). From the Middle Ages, dried cod from Norway's Lofoten Islands was exported in large quantities to Mediterranean countries, because it could be kept for years and was suited to eating on Catholic fast days when meat was not eaten. The people of Monaco and Nice stewed the dried cod with Mediterranean tomatoes and olives, forming a local specialty that reflects the trade between northern Europe and the Mediterranean in the Middle Ages.

ranking.name: Monegasque sweet fougasse
ranking.description: A flat sweet bread baked from fermented dough with orange blossom water, sugar and aniseed, sprinkled with colored sugar granules. It has a soft, sweet texture with the delicate fragrance of orange blossom and anise.
ranking.history: Fougasse comes from the ancient Roman panis focacius (hearth bread) and developed various versions in Provence and Liguria. The Monegasque version adds orange blossom water and anise to make a sweet festive bread, traditionally eaten on National Day, 19 November, and the red and white colored sugar granules on top symbolize the colors of the Monaco flag.

ranking.name: Pan bagnat (Nice sandwich)
ranking.description: A sandwich of a round bun filled with tuna, boiled egg, tomato, olives, onion and anchovies, drizzled with olive oil. The bread absorbs the olive oil and vegetable juices, giving a moist texture.
ranking.history: Pan bagnat means "bathed bread" and comes from Nice, originally a simple lunch in which fishermen and laborers soaked day-old bread with water and added salad ingredients, similar to a Niçoise salad in bread. Monaco and Nice belong to the same cultural sphere on the border of Liguria and Provence (Nice was only annexed to France in 1860), so the food of the two places is similar, and today it is a common picnic food on the beaches of the Riviera.
